title: KV subpage allocation + Healer background defrag strategy for GPU memory
creator: Sofia Patel
description: Problem: Live KV caches on GPUs are suffering long-tail memory fragmentation due to heterogeneous key/value sizes and churn from streaming workloads. Fragmentation increases per-request memory pressure, causes artificial OOMs under load, and reduces effective cache capacity, which in turn worsens batching efficiency. Goal: Implement a low-overhead allocation strategy (subpage allocation + slotted arenas) combined with an in-GPU "Healer" background defragmenter that cooperatively relocates cold/fragmented slots without impacting latency SLOs. Approach: 1) Allocation: introduce 4 subpage sizes per slab class (tiny/compact/standard/large) with fixed-slot headers and per-stream free lists to reduce cross-stream contention. Use packed metadata (16 bytes) per slot and soft indirection handles to allow movable allocations. 2) Placement: maintain per-GPU epoched region maps to quickly identify fragmentation hotspots; prefer bump allocation for hot-insert patterns and slab reuse for stable distributions. 3) Healer defragger: a low-priority GPU kernel + CPU coordinator that performs incremental compaction in micro-batches between normal inference work. It uses live-copy migration with epoch/quiesce windows and optional double-buffering for KV slots that are pinned by in-flight requests. Healer heuristics: - prioritize regions with >40% internal fragmentation or >25% free islands smaller than smallest-subpage - limit relocation bandwidth to <=5% of GPU memory bandwidth in steady-state - pause and back off when tail latency > SLO threshold 4) Indirection: add a 64-bit handle table (GPU-resident) that maps logical key IDs to current slot pointers. Handles are cheap to update during relocation and allow heals without changing client-visible references. 5) Eviction & compaction synergy: integrate eviction policy with healer so evicted slots are reclaimed immediately; healer focuses on consolidating partially-free slabs rather than touching cold LRU entries repeatedly. 6) Telemetry & rollouts: add fragmentation gauges, relocation rate, healer throttle, per-region free-run histograms, and integration with Console dashboards. Performance targets: - Reduce fragmentation-induced effective capacity loss by >=35% for mixed-size chat workloads - Maintain p99 token latency regressions < 3% during steady-state healer operation - Reduce OOM frequency on stressed Dedicated pools by >=90% Acceptance criteria: see acceptance_criteria field. Trade-offs & Risks: - Metadata overhead (handle table + headers) consumes ~1.2-1.8% GPU memory; acceptable for targeted customers but must be configurable per-deployment. - Healer relocations add extra memcpy and kernel overhead; must be carefully throttled. - Complexity of indirection may complicate checkpointing and persistence for Private deployments; we will provide opt-out config and ensure consistent snapshots. Milestones: 1) Design doc and simulation (this ticket) 2) Microbench allocator + synthetic fragmentation test 3) Healer prototype on dev-gpu pool (non-prod) 4) Integrate with eviction & batching logic 5) Canary on dedicated pool + metrics validation 6) Full rollout to hosted runtime with rollback hooks Links: Design doc (draft): https://confluence.redwood.ai/kvcache/subpage-healer-draft , Benchmark plan: https://go.redwood.ai/bench/kvcache-healer , PRs: (TBD)

acceptance_criteria: Allocator correctness: no dangling handles after relocation (verified by unit tests + fuzzing)
Healer safety: relocation can be paused and resumes without losing entries or causing inconsistent reads (integration tests)
Performance: fragmentation loss reduced >=35% on benchmark suite; p99 latency regression <3% under steady-state healer
Resource overhead: metadata overhead <=2% on 80GB GPU for default config
Operational: Console shows healer throttle, relocation rate, region fragmentation heatmap; alerts when healer backs off >5s
Rollout: successful canary on dedicated pool (min 3 nodes) for 48h with no OOMs and stable autoscaling
